If we define the functions $f$, $g$ and $h$ that map $R$ into $R$ by :

$f(x)=x^{4}, g(x)= \sqrt{x^{2}+1}, h(x)=x^{2}+72$, then the value of the composite functions $ho(gof)$ and $(hog)of$ are given as
questions.solution:
Answer: D

Source solution 1 (score: 3)

Function Composition is Associative i.e. $ho(fog) = (hog)of$ is ALWAYS True. So, we don't need to calculate these two separately. Calculate one of them & the other will also be the same.

Detailed Video Solution: Detailed Video Solution (Click Here)

Answer: D.

f(x) = $x^4$, g(x) = $\sqrt{x^2 +1}$, h(x) = $x^2 + 72$

gof = g($x^4$) = $\sqrt{x^8 +1}$

$ho(gof)$ = h($\sqrt{x^8 +1}$) = $(\sqrt{x^8 +1})^2$ +72 = $x^8 + 73$

questions.qtext: Suppose $\mathrm{f}: \mathrm{X} \rightarrow \mathrm{Y}$ is a function. Which of the following are possible?
questions.solution:
Answer: A, B, C, D

Source solution 1 (score: 3)

Suppose we are given a function $f:X \to Y$,

We are asked about the possibilities of the function being injective and/or surjective.

First let's find out what these words mean.

$ Injective $: A function is injective (one-to-one) if each possible element of the codomain is mapped to by at most one element of the domain.

$ Surjective $: A surjective function, or onto function, is a function where every element in the codomain is mapped to by at least one element from the domain. Nothing in the codomain set is left out.

Let's understand with examples, along with the importance of finiteness of the domain and codomain sets.

Option A: $f$ is injective but not surjective.
Here, let: $f: \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ be defined by:

$f(n) = n + 1$

Different values of n give different values of $f(n)$, so $f$ is injective.

However, $0$ is not in the range of $f$, so $f$ is not surjective.

Option A is possible.

(However, if we assume that the cardinalities of $X$ and $Y$ are finite and equal, i.e. $\lvert X \lvert = \lvert Y \lvert $, then it is not possible.)

Option B: $f$ is surjective but not injective.

Let's suppose an $f: \mathbb{Z}- \{0\} \to \mathbb{N} $ defined by:

$f(n) = |n|$

This function is surjective.
But it is not injective because:
$f(1) = 1$
$f(-1) = 1$

Here, multiple values of n can have the same output, i.e. one element in the codomain can have multiple values in the domain set. So $f$ is not injective.

However, every element of N has a corresponding pre-image , so $f$ is surjective.

Option B is possible.

(But if we assume that the cardinalities of $X$ and $Y$ are finite and equal, i.e. $\lvert X \lvert = \lvert Y \lvert $, then it is not possible.)

$Note: $ From the above two cases, we can conclude that if $X$ and $Y$ are finite sets with $\lvert X \lvert = \lvert Y \lvert $, then $f$ is one-one if and only if $f$ is onto, and vice versa.

Option C: f is both surjective and injective.

This happens when there is a one-to-one mapping between X and Y.

Consider $f: \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ defined by:

$f(n) = n$

Every element has exactly one preimage, so f is both injective and surjective.

Hence Option C is possible.

Option D: f is neither surjective nor injective.

Consider a function $f: \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ defined by:

$f(n) = 1$

It is not injective because different values of n give the same output.

It is also not surjective because values other than 1 are never obtained.

Option D can also be possible.

So we can conclude that all four options are possible, and the answer is all the options A, B, C, D.

questions.qtext: Define $f(n)=\frac{n}{2}+\frac{1-(-1)^{n}}{4}$ for all $n \in \mathbb{Z}$. Thus, $f: \mathbb{Z} \rightarrow \mathbb{Z}, \mathbb{Z}$ the set of all integers. Which is correct?

options.text: $f$ is not a function from $\mathbb{Z} \rightarrow \mathbb{Z}$ because $\frac{n}{2} \notin \mathbb{Z}$.
$\mathrm{f}$ is a function and is not onto but is one-to-one.
$f$ is a function and is not onto and not one-to-one
$f$ is a function and is onto but not one-to-one.

questions.solution:
Answer: D

Selected solution (score: 25)
$\text{f(n)} =\left\{\begin{matrix} \large{\frac{n}{2}}, & \text{n is even}\\ \large{\frac{n +1}{2}}, & \text{ n is odd} \end{matrix}\right.$

$\text{1) f(3) = f(4) = 2, so f is not a one-one function.}$

$\text{2) for any y }\in \mathbb{Z}, \text{for f(x) = y the value of x is either x = 2y(x is even) or x = 2y - 1( x is odd) }$.

$\text{so every y in co-domain has a pre-image so function f is onto}$.

So option D is true.

questions.qtext: Let $f : X \to Y$ and $g : Y \to Z$. Let $h = g \circ f : X \to Z$. Suppose $g$ is one-to-one and onto. Which of the following is FALSE?

options.text: If $f$ is one-to-one then $h$ is one-to-one and onto.
If $f$ is not onto then $h$ is not onto.
If $f$ is not one-to-one then $h$ is not one-to-one.

questions.solution:
Answer: A

Selected solution (score: 9)
$\text{A)}$ $\text{f:}$ $\mathbb{R}^+\cup \set{0} \mapsto \mathbb{R}$ such that $\text{f(x)} = x^2$, $\text{f}$ is one-one.

$\text{g:}$ $\mathbb{R} \mapsto \mathbb{R}$ such that $\text{g(x)} = x^3$, $\text{g}$ is bijective.

$\text{g}\circ \text{f:} $ $\mathbb{R}^+\cup \set{0} \mapsto \mathbb{R}$ such that $\text{gof(x)} = x^6$, $\text{g}\circ \text{f}$ is one-one and its not onto.

so Option A is false.



$\text{B) if f is not onto then g }\circ \text{f is not onto}.$

$\text{Proof}$:- Assume $\text{f}$ is not onto.

$\text{(implies)} \mapsto \exists\text{y}_1\in\text{Y}$ $\forall \text{x}\in\text{X ( f(x)}\neq\text{y )}.$

Since $\text{g}$ is bijective there exists a unique $\text{z}_1 \in \text{Z such that } \mathrm{g}\text{(y}_1\text{)} = \text{z}_1.$

$\text{(implies)} \mapsto \text{for such z}_1 \text{ there is no x}_1 \in \text{X such that g(f(x}_1\text{)) = z}_1 $.

$\text{(implies)} \mapsto \exists\text{z}_1\in\text{Z}$ $\forall \text{x}\in\text{X ( g(f(x))}\neq\text{z}_1 ).$

$\text{(implies)} \mapsto \text{g} \circ \text{f is not onto.} $

$\text{so if f is not onto then g }\circ \text{f is not onto}.$

$ $

$\text{C) if f is not one-one then g }\circ \text{f is not one-one}.$

$\text{Proof}$:- Assume $\text{f}$ is not one-one..

$\text{(implies)} \mapsto \exists\text{x}_1\in\text{X}$ $\exists\text{x}_2\in\text{X} \text{(x}_1\neq\text{x}_2 \wedge\text{ f(x}_1\text{)} = \text{ f(x}_2\text{)} \text{)}$

Since the range of function $\text{f}$ is subset of domain of function $\text{g}$, for such an $\text{x}_1 \text{ and x}_2,$ $\text{ g(f(x}_1\text{))} = \text{ g(f(x}_2\text{)} \text{))}$

$\text{(implies)} \mapsto \text{g} \circ \text{f is not one-one.} $

$\text{so if f is not one-one then g }\circ \text{f is not one-one}.$

$ $

$\text{D) if f is one-one then g }\circ \text{f is one-one}.$

$\text{Proof}$:- Assume $\text{f}$ is one-one and $\text{g} \circ \text{f}$ is not one-one.

$\text{(implies)} \mapsto \exists\text{x}_1\in\text{X}$ $\exists\text{x}_2\in\text{X} \text{(x}_1\neq\text{x}_2 \wedge\text{ g(f(x}_1\text{))} = \text{ g(f(x}_2\text{))} \text{)}$

Since g is a bijective function $\text{f(x}_1\text{)} = \text{f(x}_2\text{)}$ $\text{(otherwise g is not one-one)}$

$\text{(implies)} \mapsto \exists\text{x}_1\in\text{X}$ $\exists\text{x}_2\in\text{X} \text{(x}_1\neq\text{x}_2 \wedge\text{ f(x}_1\text{)} = \text{ f(x}_2\text{)} \text{)}$

$\text{(implies)} \mapsto \text{f is not one-one}$.

which is a $\text{CONTRADICTION}$.

so by proof by contradiction, $\text{if f is one-one then g }\circ \text{f is one-one}.$



So Option A is the answer.
Source solution 2 (score: 0)

The statement

$$
\text{If } f \text{ is one-to-one, then } h \text{ is one-to-one and onto.}
$$

is false.

Since $g$ is injective and $f$ is injective, $h=g\circ f$ is one-to-one.

However, $h$ need not be onto unless $f$ is also onto.

Counterexample:

Let

$$
X=\{1\},\qquad
Y=\{a,b\},\qquad
Z=\{0,1\}.
$$

Let $g:Y\to Z$ be the bijection

$$
g(a)=0,\qquad g(b)=1.
$$

Let

$$
f(1)=a.
$$

Then $f$ is one-to-one.

$g$ is bijective.

$h(1)=0$, so $h$ is not onto (it misses $1$).

Therefore, the statement is false.
Some observations:

If $g$ is bijective and $h=g\circ f$ is onto, then $f$ is onto.

If $g$ is bijective and $h=g\circ f$ is one-to-one, then $f$ is one-to-one.

If $g$ is bijective and $h=g\circ f$ is bijective, then $f$ is bijective.

If $g$ is bijective and $f$ is onto, then $h=g\circ f$ is onto.

If $g$ is bijective and $f$ is one-to-one, then $h=g\circ f$ is one-to-one.

If $g$ is bijective and $f$ is bijective, then $h=g\circ f$ is bijective.

A compact summary: If \(g\) is bijective, then composition with \(g\) preserves injectivity, surjectivity, and bijectivity. In other words, \[ \begin{aligned} g\circ f \text{ is onto} &\iff f \text{ is onto},\\ g\circ f \text{ is one-to-one} &\iff f \text{ is one-to-one},\\ g\circ f \text{ is bijective} &\iff f \text{ is bijective}. \end{aligned} \]

questions.qtext: Let $\mathrm{g}: \mathrm{A} \rightarrow \mathrm{B}$ and $\mathrm{f}: \mathrm{B} \rightarrow \mathrm{C}$ be functions. If $\mathrm{f} \circ \mathrm{g}$ is bijective, then which of the following must be true?
questions.solution:
Answer: A

Source solution 1 (score: 8)

If \( fog \) is bijective, it means that the composition function \( fog \) is both injective (one-to-one) and surjective (onto).

For a function \( fog \) to be bijective, it must satisfy the following:

1. $Injective$: Every element in the codomain of \( fog \) has $at$ $most$ one pre-image in the domain of \( fog \).


2. $Surjective$: Every element in the codomain of \( fog \) has at $least$ one pre-image in the domain of \( fog \).

Given \( fog \) is bijective, let's analyze the options:

A. \( g \) is one-to-one (injective):


This must be true. If \( g \) were not one-to-one, there would be at least one element in \( A \) mapping to the same element in \( B \), which would violate the injective property of \( fog \).

B. \( g \) is onto (surjective):


This does not have to be true. While it's possible for \( g \) to be onto, it's not a requirement for \( fog \) to be bijective. \( fog \) could still be bijective even if \( g \) is not onto, as long as it's one-to-one.

C. \( f \) is one-to-one (injective):


This does not have to be true. While \( f \) being one-to-one is $not$ $sufficient$ for \( fog \) to be bijective. \( fog \) could still be bijective even if \( f \) is not one-to-one.

D. \( f \) is onto (surjective):


This must be true. If \( f \) were not onto, there would be at least one element in the codomain of \( fog \) that does not have a pre-image in the domain of \( f \), which would violate the surjective property of \( fog \).

So, the correct answer is:
A. \( g \) is one-to-one.
D. \( f \) is onto.

Source solution 2 (score: 3)
Suppose $\text{g}$ is function from $\text{A} \mapsto \text{B}$ and $\text{f}$ is function from $\text{B} \mapsto \text{C}$ then $\text{f} \circ \text{g :} \text{ A} \mapsto \text{C}$

Statement 1:- If $\text{f} \circ \text{g}$ is onto then so $\text{f}$.

$\text{Proof}$:- Assume $\text{f} \circ \text{g}$ is onto.

Suppose $\text{c is an arbitary element from the set } \text{C}$.

$\text{(implies) }\mapsto \text{Since f(g(x)) is onto }\exists\text{a}\in\text{A}\text{( f(g(a) = c) }$.

Since the Range of function g is subset of $\text{B}$, $\forall \text{a} \in \text{A }$$\text{g(a) = b} \text{ for some b} \in \text{B}$

$\text{(implies) }\mapsto \exists\text{b}\in\text{B}\text{( f(b) = c) }$

$\text{(implies) } \mapsto \text{ for any arbitary c} \in \text{C}$ $ \exists\text{b}\in\text{B}\text{( f(b) = c) }$

$\text{(implies) } \mapsto \text{f is onto}.$

so $\text{f} \circ \text{g is onto then f is onto}.$

$ $

Statement 2:- if $\text{f} \circ \text{g}$ is one-one then so is $\text{g}$.

$\text{Proof}$:- Assume $\text{f} \circ \text{g}$ is one-one and $\text{g}$ is not one-one/

$\text{(implies) } \mapsto \exists\text{a}_1 \in A \exists\text{a}_2 \in A (\text{a}_1\neq\text{a}_2 \wedge g(\text{a}_1) = g(\text{a}_2).$

$\text{(implies) } \mapsto \text{for such a}_1 \text{ and a}_2, (\text{f} \circ \text{g})(\text{a}_1 )= (\text{f} \circ \text{g})(\text{a}_2).$

$\text{(implies) } \mapsto \text{f} \circ \text{g} \text{ is not one-one }.$

which is a $\text{CONTRADICTION}$

so by proof by contradiction, if $\text{f} \circ \text{g}$ is one-one then so is $\text{g}$.

$ $

Since $\text{f} \circ \text{g}$ is bijective, option A , D are True.

To contradict the option B, C check this example:

$\text{g} : \mathbb{R}^+\cup \set{0} \mapsto \mathbb{R} \text{ such that } \text{g(x) = }\sqrt(x), \text{g is one-one and g is not onto.} $

$\text{f} : \mathbb{R} \mapsto \mathbb{R}^+\cup \set{0} \text{ such that } \text{f(x) = x}^2, \text{f is onto and f is not one-one.} $

then $\text{f} \circ \text{g}: \mathbb{R}^+\cup \set{0} \mapsto \mathbb{R}^+\cup \set{0} \text{ such that } (\text{f} \circ \text{g})(x) = \text{ x}$

$\text{we can clearly see that } \text{f} \circ \text{g is bijective but still g is not onto and f is not one-one}. $

$ $

So options A, D are True.
